title: Psalm 48: Great Is the LORD in the City of Our God
summary: The psalm praises the LORD in Zion, his holy mountain, the joy of all the earth. Kings who gathered against the city saw it, panicked, and fled, and the worshipers in the temple reflect on God's loving devotion and righteous judgments. They are invited to walk around Zion, count its towers, and study its defenses, so they can tell the next generation that this God is their God forever.
story: Psalm 48 completes the trio of Zion psalms that began with Psalm 46. There God was a refuge within the city; in Psalm 47 he was enthroned over all nations; here the worshipers stand inside Zion itself and marvel. The story of the Bible gives Jerusalem a central role: it is the place God chose for his name, where David's heir reigned and the temple stood. Later the city would fall to Babylon, and that fall tested the confidence of songs like this one. The psalm's final lines already look past the stones to the God they point to.
historical:
The heading calls it "A song" and "A Psalm of the sons of Korah", placing it among the temple singers' repertoire. The event behind verses 4 to 7, when kings assembled against the city and fled, is not named. Some link it with Sennacherib's failed siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC (2 Kings 18 and 19). Others point to 2 Chronicles 20, where a coalition of Moab, Ammon, and others marched against Jehoshaphat and destroyed one another, and where Korahite Levites are said to have stood up to praise God (2 Chronicles 20:19). Many scholars think the psalm is less a report of one battle than a liturgical celebration of God's protection, using stock images of enemy kings routed before Zion that also appear in Psalms 2 and 76.

The psalm reflects the period of the Davidic kings, when the temple stood and the city's walls, towers, and citadels were visible signs of security. After 587 or 586 BC, when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, the psalm would have been read with grief, and later with the hope of restoration.
cultural:
Verse 2 compares Mount Zion to "the peaks of Zaphon". Zaphon (the word also means north) was the name of a mountain in northern Syria, today called Jebel Aqra, which Canaanite texts from Ugarit describe as the home of the storm god Baal. By using the name for Zion, a modest hill, the psalm makes a bold claim: the true mountain of God is not Baal's peak but the place where the LORD dwells.

The ships of Tarshish (verse 7) were large, seagoing trading vessels, named after a distant port whose location is debated (southern Spain is a common proposal). They stood for wealth and human power, and Isaiah names them among the proud things God will humble (Isaiah 2:16). The east wind, blowing hot and violent from the desert, was a familiar instrument of God's judgment in the Old Testament. Walking around a city and counting its towers was a way of inspecting and celebrating its strength; here it becomes an act of teaching the next generation.
literary: The psalm moves like a procession. Verses 1 to 3 praise God and his city. Verses 4 to 8 tell the story of the kings who came and fled, using quick, breathless verbs ("They saw and were astounded; they fled in terror") and the image of a woman in labor for sudden anguish. Verse 8 is a hinge: "As we have heard, so we have seen", where what the fathers reported has now been witnessed. Verses 9 to 11 turn to worship inside the temple, and verses 12 to 14 send the worshipers around the walls with a command to tell the next generation. The psalm begins and ends with God, not the city: "Great is the LORD" and "this God is our God".

outline.t: The great God and his beautiful city
The kings who came and fled
Reflecting on God's love in the temple
Walk around Zion and tell the next generation

doctrines.note: The psalm praises the city only because God is in it. Its last line, "this God is our God forever and ever", makes clear that the walls are witnesses to God, not substitutes for him.

The command to inspect the city "that you may tell the next generation" shows faith as something passed down. Remembering God's acts and telling them to children was central to Israel's life (Deuteronomy 6:6-7).
God's judgments make Zion glad (verse 11). His judging is good news for those who trust him: he sets things right, overturning proud kings and ships alike.

words.note: Tsiyyon, Zion. Originally the name of the Jebusite stronghold David captured (2 Samuel 5:7), it came to mean the temple mount and Jerusalem as a whole, and then God's people and their future hope. In this psalm it is both a real place and a symbol of God's dwelling.

Tsaphon, Zaphon, a mountain in the far north known in Canaanite religion as the seat of Baal. Calling Zion "like the peaks of Zaphon" takes the language of a rival religion and reassigns it to the LORD.

Chesed, loving devotion or steadfast love, God's loyal love within his covenant. In verse 9 the worshipers "contemplate" it in the temple. The rescue of the city is read not as luck but as an act of this covenant love.

christ: The link to Christ is thematic, since the New Testament does not quote this psalm. Jesus once called Jerusalem "the city of the great King" (Matthew 5:35), echoing verse 2. Yet he also wept over the city and foretold the destruction of its temple, which came in AD 70. The New Testament moves the hope of Zion from the earthly city to the heavenly one: Hebrews 12:22 says believers have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, and Revelation 21 describes the new Jerusalem, whose temple is the Lord God and the Lamb. The psalm's final turn from walls to God himself prepares for that move.

hard.q: The psalm says God will establish Zion forever, but Jerusalem fell to Babylon and later to Rome. Was the psalm wrong?
hard.a: Some in Judah before the exile treated songs like this as a guarantee that Jerusalem could never fall, and Jeremiah rebuked that confidence (Jeremiah 7:4). The psalm itself grounds the city's security in God's presence and loving devotion, not in its walls, and the prophets insisted that God could leave a city that abandoned him. Many readers therefore hear "forever" as belonging to God's commitment to his dwelling among his people, which survived the fall of the earthly city. Jewish readers kept the hope of a restored Zion; Christians see it fulfilled and still to be fulfilled in the heavenly Jerusalem. Both readings take the promise seriously without making it a guarantee for stones.

questions: "As we have heard, so we have seen." Where have you seen for yourself what you had only heard about God?
The worshipers count towers in order to tell the next generation. What do you want the next generation to know about God, and how will they learn it?
Why is it dangerous to trust a holy place, a church, or a tradition in place of the God it points to?
